content: Clioquinol and hydrocortisone cream is a topical medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of various dermatological conditions, including dermatitis, stasis dermatitis, pyoderma, nuchal eczema, chronic eczematoid otitis externa, acne, urticata, localized or disseminated neurodermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus, anogenital pruritus (vulvae, scroti, ani), folliculitis, and bacterial dermatoses. Common adverse reactions include rash and hypersensitivity. For adults, the cream is applied in a thin layer to the affected area three or four times daily. The FDA has classified its indications as possibly effective for conditions such as contact or atopic dermatitis, impetiginized eczema, nummular eczema, infantile eczema, endogenous chronic infectious dermatitis, stasis dermatitis, pyoderma, nuchal eczema, chronic eczematoid otitis externa, acne urticata, localized or disseminated neurodermatitis, lichen simplex chronicus, anogenital pruritus, folliculitis, bacterial dermatoses, mycotic dermatoses (e.g., tinea capitis, cruris, corporis, pedis), moniliasis, and intertrigo. However, further investigation is required to finalize the classification of less-than-effective indications. Off-label uses in adults include acne urticata, candidiasis, dermatitis, mycotic skin disorders, eczema, folliculitis, intertrigo, lichen simplex chronicus, anogenital pruritus, pyoderma, and minor superficial bacterial skin infections. In pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding FDA-labeled indications and dosages. Off-label use is also not well-documented. Special care must be taken when using this medication in children, as it is not recommended for infants or children under two years of age. Chronic corticosteroid therapy in children may interfere with growth and development, and therapy exceeding two weeks or involving more than two daily applications should be carefully evaluated. Application to more than 5-10% of the body surface or under occlusive dressings (e.g., tight-fitting diapers) should be avoided. Contraindications include intolerance to iodochlorhydroxyquin, hydrocortisone, chloroxine, iodine, iodine-containing preparations, or related compounds. It should not be used in cases of herpes simplex, vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum, varicella, or other viral skin infections. Warnings include the potential for adverse reactions such as rash, hypersensitivity, skin thinning, easy bruising, burning, itching, irritation, dryness, folliculitis, blistering, peeling, redness, swelling, hypertrichosis, acneiform eruptions, hypopigmentation, perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, skin maceration, secondary infection, skin atrophy, striae, and miliaria. Therapy should be discontinued if any untoward reaction occurs. There is limited information on drug interactions, monitoring, and pharmacology. The mechanism of action of iodochlorhydroxyquin is not fully understood, but it is known to have broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal properties. Topical corticosteroids exhibit anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive actions, though the exact mechanism of their anti-inflammatory activity is unclear. During pregnancy, clioquinol and hydrocortisone cream is classified as Category C by the FDA. While topical steroids have not been reported to adversely affect pregnancy, their safety has not been definitively established. Use of large amounts or prolonged application is not recommended due to potential systemic absorption. Animal studies have shown teratogenic effects with potent corticosteroids. The cream should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. For nursing mothers, it is unknown whether topical administration results in systemic absorption sufficient to produce detectable quantities in breast milk. Systemically administered corticosteroids are secreted into breast milk in quantities unlikely to harm the infant, but caution is advised. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of this cream in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or those with renal or hepatic impairment. Similarly, there is no guidance for use in immunocompromised patients. The cream is administered topically, and occlusive dressings may enhance percutaneous absorption, which can be beneficial for resistant dermatoses. However, systemic absorption of topical corticosteroids follows similar pharmacokinetic pathways to systemically administered corticosteroids, with metabolism primarily occurring in the liver and excretion via the kidneys and bile. In cases of suspected overdose, contact the National Poison Help hotline immediately.
